source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 different LLMs, aggregated by the median, forecast about as well as a crowd of 925 humans. It beat the 50% no-information baseline.
numbers: 31 binary Metaculus questions, Oct 2023 to Jan 2024. LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.85. Equivalence test at d=0.5 (0.081 Brier) passed. Best single model GPT-4 0.15; worst Coral 0.38.
limits: Only 31 questions. Web interfaces, default settings, 3 queries per model. Equivalence test not preregistered. Training-cutoff contamination not controlled (Douven 2026 shows this matters).
agent_relevance: Supports mixing different models in S7, but the gain comes from model diversity, not from repeated draws of one model.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Models showed acquiescence bias: mean forecasts sat above 50% while fewer than half the questions resolved yes. The median aggregate did not fix calibration; the aggregate was overconfident.
numbers: Calibration plot (Fig 8): aggregate overpredicts. The median still beat the baseline despite the bias.
limits: Question mix skews negative, so part of the bias may be base rate.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a pooled probability as calibrated. Use agreement only as a hint (matches G4).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Showing the human median to a model improved its forecast, but plain averaging of model and human forecast was better still. The models moved toward the human number rather than weighing evidence.
limits: Two models only. Models were told the human median.
agent_relevance: If our agent shows a candidate answer to a second pass, expect copying, not weighing. Combine by code, not by asking the model to update.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval plus reasoning system gets close to the human crowd. Its ensemble uses a trimmed mean, which beat mean, median, geometric mean and a self-consistency variant on validation.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (random 0.25); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Averaging system and crowd gave 0.146. Table 3: system beat the crowd only in some subsets (5+ articles: system 0.238 vs crowd 0.240); the average of system and crowd was best in every setting.
limits: Questions from forecasting platforms after model cutoffs. System tuned on a validation set. Crowd still better overall.
agent_relevance: The pooling rule was a small choice; trimmed mean was best. Model calibration was already good, so extremizing and recalibration were not needed (see next line).

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Standard calibration fixes (binning, isotonic regression) did not improve the ensemble. The system was naturally well calibrated.
numbers: Fig 3: calibration near the diagonal on validation and test. Final system uses GPT-4-1106-Preview plus fine-tuned GPT-4-0613; the former gave 0.01 to 0.03 lower Brier than alternatives.
limits: Specific to this retrieval pipeline. Schoenegger saw overconfidence in a different setup.
agent_relevance: Do not add post-hoc extremizing or recalibration to votes without a held-out check (consistent with G4: no extremizing votes).

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Superforecasters beat the public and every LLM. A 3-model by 3-prompt LLM ensemble baseline (9 forecasts; median, geometric mean, geometric mean of log odds) was built, but top LLMs still trailed.
numbers: 200-question human subset: superforecasters Brier 0.096, public 0.121, best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122, p<0.001. Best LLM without crowd forecast access 0.136. Dataset-only subset: superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. Candidate single-model scratchpad Briers: Claude 3.5 0.178, GPT-4o 0.207, Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.214.
limits: Top LLMs saw the human crowd forecast on market questions. Only 39 superforecasters.
agent_relevance: Aggregating LLMs does not close the gap to expert humans. Treat model ensembles as a floor, not a ceiling.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: The paper reports a linear link between Brier score and Chatbot Arena rank or log training compute, and extrapolates a crossing with superforecasters.
numbers: Figure 1: linear fits of overall Brier vs Arena score and vs log compute.
limits: Extrapolation, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: No direct use for S7.

source: Wang, Wei, Schuurmans, Le, Chi et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the majority answer raises accuracy a lot. This is the first large Condorcet-style use in LLMs. Weighting votes by model probability was worse than a plain vote.
numbers: PaLM-540B: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9. Table 1 plain majority: GSM8K 74.4, MultiArith 99.3, AQuA 48.3, SVAMP 86.6, CSQA 80.7, ARC-c 88.7. Unnormalised probability-weighted sum GSM8K 59.9; normalised 74.1. 40 samples, mean of 10 runs; gains saturate quickly.
limits: Samples come from one model, so errors are correlated, not independent. Needs a short closed-form answer.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S7 vote in code. Plain count beat likelihood weights, so keep the rule simple.

source: Li, Zhang, Yu, Fu, Ye (2024) More Agents Is All You Need
finding: Sampling-and-voting (Agent Forest) raises accuracy with ensemble size, and gains grow with task difficulty. A small model with voting beat a larger single model.
numbers: Gains: GSM8K +12 to 24 points, MATH +6 to 10, MMLU +5 to 11, Chess +1 to 4, HumanEval +4 to 9. Llama2-13B with ensemble 59% on GSM8K vs Llama2-70B single 54%. Combined with other methods: GSM8K +10 to 21.
limits: Chess with Llama2-13B/70B and debate was an exception for stacked methods. Gains shrink on easy tasks and the curve flattens. Samples from one model are not independent.
agent_relevance: Spend votes on hard items, not easy ones (matches G12). Voting is orthogonal to other scaffolds, so it can sit at S7 after S4.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
finding: Where answers are free text and cannot be matched, USC asks the model to pick the most consistent candidate. It is reported to match standard self-consistency on math, match execution-based consistency on code without running code, and work on open-ended QA and summarization.
numbers: Exact scores not extracted this session (read abstract and introduction only).
limits: The model chooses, so it is an LLM judge and may carry its own bias (see Verga 2024). Same-model candidates are correlated.
agent_relevance: For open mode in S7, use USC only as a hint; prefer code grouping where output can run.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (some sample is right) keeps rising log-linearly with samples, but picking the right one by majority vote or a reward model stops improving after several hundred samples. Verifier-based selection keeps scaling.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250. CodeContests with Gemma-2B: coverage 0.02% to 7.1% with 10,000 samples (over 300x). Majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples.
limits: Domains with no verifier gain far less. Numbers are from the abstract and introduction.
agent_relevance: The case for a code-run check at S4 and S7: voting caps out, tests do not. Supports harvesting plus testing.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: LLM errors are strongly correlated across models. When two models are both wrong, they give the same wrong answer far more often than chance. More accurate models are more correlated.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 HuggingFace questions and 71 LLMs on 14,042 Helm questions. Mean agreement when both wrong: 0.423 (HuggingFace) and about 0.60 (Helm); chance 0.127 and 0.333. 100% of HF pairs and 97.5% of Helm pairs above chance. Llama 3.2-90B vs 3.1-70B agree 0.97; two apparently unrelated Helm models agree on 0.9987 of joint errors. Regression explains 34% to 62% of variation.
limits: Multiple choice only. Agreement on errors is partly forced by small answer sets.
agent_relevance: The Condorcet independence assumption fails across vendors too, not only within one model. G4 is justified by data; vote count cannot be read as evidence.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Because errors are shared, an LLM judge inflates the score of weaker models and under-scores stronger ones. In hiring, correlated rankers leave many applicants excluded.
numbers: Judge inflation is positive for models less accurate than the judge (Helm Fig 2). With 20 firms each using a random LLM, about 20% of applicants stay systemically excluded, vs near 0 under random preferences. 20 LLMs, 1,800 resume pairs.
limits: Resume task uses human ratings as truth; one pool of 20 models.
agent_relevance: An agent that checks its answer with the same model family will mostly agree with itself. Use code or a different family for S8 checks.

source: Zhang and Martinez (2026) Beta-Binomial Latent Class Model for Correlated Repeated Judgments
finding: Repeated samples of the same item from one model are highly correlated, so ten samples carry little more information than one or two. Models that assume independence are overconfident and biased.
numbers: 52,500 judgments, 7 open models 1B to 32B, 3 prompts, 10 samples per item. Intraclass correlation 0.50 to 0.93; ten ratings equal 1.07 to 1.81 independent ratings. Binomial latent class 95% intervals missed the human-label value in 42 of 42 settings and underestimated total error in 42 of 42. Beta-binomial fix raised coverage to 0.90.
limits: Classification task with human labels, small open models. Not about reasoning chains.
agent_relevance: Gives the effective sample size of a vote: far fewer than N. Do not count more draws as more evidence (G4); change the model, prompt or tool instead.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?
finding: Most of the benefit of multi-agent debate comes from the majority vote, not from the discussion. They prove debate alone is a martingale on expected correctness.
numbers: 7 benchmarks, 5 agents. Qwen2.5-7B average: single 0.7205, debate (decentralised, 2 rounds) 0.7377, majority vote 0.7691. Llama3.1-8B: single 0.6203, vote 0.7242. More debate rounds lowered the Qwen average (0.7377 at 2 rounds to 0.7050 at 5). Arithmetics: single 0.814, debate 0.76, vote 0.99.
limits: Small instruct models. A bias toward correction (MAD-oracle) lifted the Qwen average to 0.8236, but that uses an oracle.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate). Use a vote or a code test; do not add discussion between samples.

source: Kaesberg, Becker, Wahle, Ruas, Gipp (2025) Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Which decision rule is best depends on task type: voting rules did better on reasoning, consensus rules on knowledge. More agents helped; more discussion rounds before the decision hurt.
numbers: 7 protocols, one variable changed at a time. Voting improved reasoning tasks by 13.2% over other protocols (paper text: +13.1% SQuAD 2.0, +0.2% StrategyQA, +26.4% MuSR); consensus improved knowledge tasks by 2.8% (+2.3% MMLU, +4.9% MMLU-Pro, +1.3% GPQA over the voting average). All-Agents Drafting up to +3.3%, Collective Improvement up to +7.4%. Approval voting often failed to reach a decision.
limits: Small differences on knowledge tasks. The paper text says agents are agreeable, so consensus is reached quickly.
agent_relevance: Choose the aggregation rule by task class in S7. Drafting independent answers before any sharing keeps votes closer to independent.

source: Verga et al. (2024) Replacing Judges with Juries: Evaluating LLM Generations with a Panel of Diverse Models
finding: A panel of three smaller models from different families agreed with humans better than one GPT-4 judge, showed less self-preference bias, and cost 7 to 8 times less.
numbers: Pearson / Kendall tau vs humans: PoLL 0.917 / 0.778; GPT-4 0.817 / 0.667; GPT-3.5 0.883 / 0.730. Std of score deviation from humans: PoLL 2.2, GPT-3.5 6.1. Largest positive deviation arises when a model judges itself. Cost per judge run: $1.25 in / $4.25 out vs $10 / $30. PoLL kappa row 0.763, 0.906, 0.867 on single-hop QA sets.
limits: Judging tasks with a reference answer. Three judges is a small jury; the panel was chosen, not sampled.
agent_relevance: Diverse-family voting beats a single strong judge at S8 and for open-mode S7. Matches the Condorcet need for independent errors.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
finding: 15 LLMs on prediction-market questions: learned aggregation beat every single model and every classical aggregator. Logistic regression was about as good as a neural net, so the gain is a weighted linear mix. Learned weights followed how little a model's errors overlapped with others, not how good it was alone.
numbers: 254 binary questions (208 initial, 94 clean after all cutoffs). Clean subset: logistic regression Brier 0.241, MLP 0.264, arithmetic mean 0.313, median 0.343 (mean beat median here). Learned weights correlate +0.482 with error decorrelation and -0.075 with individual Brier.
limits: Aggregator needs resolved training questions. Preprint-style ACM manuscript; one question source (Manifold).
agent_relevance: Weighting by independence, not accuracy, is the right pooling logic under correlation. For us, favour a candidate from a different strategy over a repeat of the best one.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds
finding: Training-cutoff leaks inflate model skill. The cloud-versus-local gap shrank on questions after every cutoff, and model rankings were only moderately stable. Even at cutoff, the LLM mean was about twice the market's Brier.
numbers: Cloud crowd (10 models) vs local crowd (5) arithmetic mean Brier 0.254 vs 0.345 on the full set (35.8% gap); 0.312 vs 0.340 on the clean subset (8.9% gap).
limits: Affects earlier crowd studies, including the 12-model 2024 study.
agent_relevance: Any internal test of vote strength must use items past the model's cutoff.

source: The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds (2026 preprint; authors not extracted)
finding: Having LLMs from different families deliberate in small groups gave a better collective estimate than just averaging their independent answers. Three copies of the same model gained nothing from deliberating.
numbers: Study 1 (jar disks, 14 photos): squared error of group consensus 0.164 vs within-group average 0.195 (Wilcoxon z=5.33, d=0.40); individual error fell from 0.230 to 0.159 after deliberation. Clone groups: Anthropic d=0.087, OpenAI d=0.144, Google d=0.062, all n.s. with Bayes factors 3.99 to 6.19 for the null; heterogeneous vs clones z=3.61, d=0.48. Best single model (Gemini) with copies of itself beat the heterogeneous consensus (d=0.88).
limits: 4 domains (numeric estimation, ML peer review, malicious-behaviour detection, sports forecasting). Peer-review result was weak in one test (p=0.86). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Contrasts with Choi 2025 (debate adds nothing): deliberation helps only with diverse models. For a one-model agent, deliberation among copies is not worth tokens (G9, G4).

source: Han et al. (2026) Conformity Dynamics in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: The Roles of Topology and Self-Social Weighting
finding: In LLM networks, agents adjust toward the majority. A confidence-weighted pooling rule with some self-weight gives better final accuracy; hub-and-spoke aggregation depends on the hub.
numbers: Star topology, GPT-3.5: hub accuracy 0.67 at self-weight 0 to 0.80 at 0.75. Ring m=2 to complete graph m=6 at self-weight 0.25: 0.70 to 0.75. Without confidence weighting accuracy fell in all topologies.
limits: Misinformation detection only. LLM stated confidence is a weak signal (SCHEMA 4b), so the gain depends on this task.
agent_relevance: If the agent merges drafts, keep each draft's own answer weighted high and do not let peers overwrite it. Keep pooling rules simple.

source: He, Chen, Yang et al. (2026) Minority Sentinel: When to Overturn Majority Voting in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
finding: In 2:1 splits among three vendor models, the minority is right about one time in four. A small trained classifier on debate features can flip to the minority with 81% precision but recovers little.
numbers: 6 benchmarks, 1,754 items. 686 (39.1%) had a 2:1 split; in 175 (25.5%) the minority was correct. Vote accuracy 74.3%, oracle 84.3% (10.0 point margin). Sentinel: flip precision 81.2% (39 correct, 9 wrong flips), net gain +1.71 points (17.1% of the margin), recovery 22.3%. Always trusting the minority: net -19.16%. GPT-4o as flip judge: net -1.37%, flip precision 42.7%. Agents: GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5.
limits: Three small models with assigned roles. CommonsenseQA and MMLU-STEM had all the wrong flips (2 and 7). Preprint, one lab.
agent_relevance: Majority is not a safe default when errors correlate. A code-side signal (a test or a run) is needed to pick the minority; an LLM judge cannot do it.

source: Karge (2026) Epistemic Filtering and Collective Hallucination: A Jury Theorem for Confidence-Calibrated Agents
finding: A Condorcet-style theorem for agents that learn their own reliability and abstain when unsure. It gives a non-asymptotic lower bound on group success and says abstention can protect against collective hallucination.
numbers: Monte Carlo simulation only; no LLM experiment in what was read (abstract and introduction).
limits: Needs agents with fixed competence and independent votes. LLM self-confidence is weak (SCHEMA 4b).
agent_relevance: Theory for a possible abstain option in S7 voting; not evidence that it works for LLMs.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical consistency across related questions (negation, conditional, and so on) can be scored with an arbitrage metric. It correlates with forecast accuracy, but forcing consistency did not make forecasts better.
numbers: Correlation of consistency metric with Brier (arbitrage / frequentist): Conditional 0.92 / 0.87 (scraped set), Negation 0.60 / 0.67, Aggregated 0.62 / 0.85 (scraped) and 0.49 / 0.66 (NewsAPI). Some checks near zero or negative on NewsAPI (Negation -0.36 arbitrage). ArbitrageForecaster improved consistency only on the check it was tuned on, did not generalize and did not improve forecasts.
limits: Binary forecasts; several checks have few tuples. Inference-time compute helped some checks only.
agent_relevance: The nearest LLM case of the doctrinal paradox: probabilities that cannot all be true. A code check of logical links is a signal, but patching to force consistency does not improve answers.

source: Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting (2024)
finding: ReAct agents with retrieval and numeric simulation reach forecasts competitive with humans. The final forecast aggregates a collection of hierarchical ReAct agents by a weighted or trimmed mean or median.
numbers: Abstract: competitive with and in some settings better than human predictions. Numbers not extracted.
limits: Read abstract, introduction and aggregation text only.
agent_relevance: A real loop where draws from several agents are pooled by code, not by an LLM.

source: Yuan, Zhang, Yang, Prenkaj, Kasneci (2026) Probabilistic Aggregation and Targeted Embedding Optimization for Collective Moral Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Fuses continuous moral-acceptability scores from several LLMs into one reliability-weighted probability, then tunes token embeddings of outlier models toward that consensus.
numbers: Numbers not extracted.
limits: First page only. Embedding tuning is training, outside our scaffold-only rule.
agent_relevance: Shows a probabilistic pool of judgment scores across models; not usable inside our scaffold.
